content: The term catuaba refers to infusions made from the bark of various trees native to Brazil. The most commonly used barks are obtained from the trees Trichilia catigua and Erythroxylum vacciniifolium. Other catuaba preparations may utilize the bark of trees from genera or families such as Anemopaegma, Ilex, Micropholis, Phyllanthus, Secondatia, Tetragastris, and species within the Myrtaceae family. It is often claimed that catuaba is derived from the tree Erythroxylum catuaba. However, this tree was only described once, in 1904, and it is currently unclear to which tree this name referred. As a result, Erythroxylum catuaba is not recognized as a valid species (Kletter et al., 2004). Local synonyms for catuaba include Chuchuhuasha, Tatuaba, Pau de Reposta, Piratancara, and Caramuru. A commercial liquid preparation called Catuama contains multiple ingredients, one of which is catuaba derived from Trichilia catigua. In traditional Brazilian medicine, an infusion of catuaba bark is used as an aphrodisiac and a stimulant for the central nervous system. However, these claims have not been scientifically validated. A journalist for the Discovery Channel has reported that scientific journals and conference presentations have supported its use for sexual enhancement. It is believed that a group of three alkaloids found in catuaba, named catuabine A, B, and C, may enhance sexual function by stimulating the nervous system. A study conducted by Manabe et al. (1992) demonstrated that extracts from Trichilia catigua were effective in preventing potentially fatal bacterial infections and HIV infection in mice. Catuaba bark and its preparations are marketed as aphrodisiacs and remedies for erectile dysfunction, and they are available for purchase in health food stores and through online retailers.
